---
title: "The brainstem nucleus that fails first"
description: "In Parkinson's disease, the locus coeruleus degenerates before the substantia nigra. In ME/CFS, the same nucleus may fail — without degenerating."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-10-01"
categories: [Cross-links, Noradrenergic, Mechanisms]
---

There is a small nucleus in the brainstem — the locus coeruleus — that is the brain's main source of norepinephrine. It is also unusually vulnerable.

In Parkinson's disease, the locus coeruleus is affected *before* the dopamine-producing substantia nigra, and human imaging now uses neuromelanin-sensitive MRI to track its integrity; one Parkinson's subtype shows early degeneration of both nuclei (@Zhou2023PDtrajectories).

**The ME/CFS parallel — and the crucial difference.** The selective norepinephrine deficit of ME/CFS shows a metabolite pattern consistent with locus-coeruleus involvement (norepinephrine down, dopamine preserved) — the same *kind* of pattern seen early in Parkinson's. But no one has examined the ME/CFS locus coeruleus at the resolution needed to detect degeneration: no imaging or post-mortem study has looked. So degeneration has not been *ruled out* — it simply has not been demonstrated. If the failure is functional (underperforming rather than dying), that would be a different and more hopeful situation.

**Why the distinction matters.** Degeneration is largely irreversible; functional failure is, in principle, reversible. Whether the ME/CFS failure is functional or degenerative is untested — the test would be 7T neuromelanin imaging, which should show *normal* locus-coeruleus volume if the failure is functional, unlike in Parkinson's.

**The caveats.** This parallel is an inference; no one has imaged the locus coeruleus in ME/CFS at this resolution. And the underlying norepinephrine finding is single-centre and unreplicated.
